idiom_name: hand-written subscriber table of {callback, context} pairs + per-subscriber eventfd/pipe
implementation_notes: C has no callable objects and no pub-sub primitive, so the channel is a hand-written registry of {callback, context} entries guarded by a pthread mutex, with the message copied (or refcounted and frozen) once per subscriber. Asynchronous delivery gives each subscriber a pipe or eventfd(2) that the publisher writes to after enqueueing, so a slow consumer never blocks the publish path; otherwise the callbacks run synchronously on the publisher's thread. The classic structure is always justified here - the real design choices are the snapshot/dispatch discipline and the per-subscriber queue bound.
pitfalls: Dispatching while holding the registry mutex deadlocks as soon as a subscriber subscribes or unsubscribes from inside its callback; snapshot under the lock and call outside it.
One msg pointer handed to every callback aliases mutable state across subscribers; copy or freeze the payload (refcount + const) at publish time.
An eventfd/pipe write per subscriber per message can overflow; treat EAGAIN as back-pressure with a declared drop policy instead of losing wakeups silently.
